claim: Ischemic stroke is one of the leading causes of death in the world.
source: Ischemic stroke, one of the leading causes of death in the world, is accompanied by the dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which aggravates neuron damage.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about stroke as a major cause of mortality globally.

claim: Ischemic stroke is accompanied by the dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
source: Ischemic stroke, one of the leading causes of death in the world, is accompanied by the dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which aggravates neuron damage.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in stroke pathophysiology supported by scientific literature.

claim: BBB dysfunction aggravates neuron damage in ischemic stroke.
source: Ischemic stroke, one of the leading causes of death in the world, is accompanied by the dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which aggravates neuron damage.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on established understanding of BBB function and stroke pathology.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the restoration of BBB in the chronic stage after stroke remain unclear.
source: However, the mechanisms underlying the restoration of BBB in the chronic stage after stroke remain unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field, setting up the rationale for the study.

claim: Lineage tracing, RNA-seq, and immunofluorescence staining revealed endothelial cell (EC) transdifferentiation into pericytes (E-pericytes) in C57BL/6 mice after stroke.
source: Lineage tracing, RNA-seq, and immunofluorescence staining revealed endothelial cell (EC) transdifferentiation into pericytes (E-pericytes) in C57BL/6 mice after stroke.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental techniques (lineage tracing, RNA-seq, immunofluorescence) performed in the study.

claim: E-pericytes depletion by diphtheria toxin A (DTA) aggravated BBB leakage in the MCAO model.
source: E-pericytes depletion by diphtheria toxin A (DTA) aggravated BBB leakage and exacerbated neurological deficits in the MCAO model.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from the study using DTA to deplete E-pericytes.

claim: E-pericytes depletion by diphtheria toxin A (DTA) exacerbated neurological deficits in the MCAO model.
source: E-pericytes depletion by diphtheria toxin A (DTA) aggravated BBB leakage and exacerbated neurological deficits in the MCAO model.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from the study using DTA to deplete E-pericytes.

claim: Myeloid cell-driven transdifferentiation of ECs into pericytes accelerated BBB restoration after stroke via endothelial-mesenchymal transformation (EndoMT).
source: The myeloid cell-driven transdifferentiation of ECs into pericytes accelerated BBB restoration and brain self-repair after stroke via endothelial-mesenchymal transformation (EndoMT).
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by experimental data showing the role of myeloid cells and EndoMT.

claim: Myeloid cell-driven transdifferentiation of ECs into pericytes accelerated brain self-repair after stroke via endothelial-mesenchymal transformation (EndoMT).
source: The myeloid cell-driven transdifferentiation of ECs into pericytes accelerated BBB restoration and brain self-repair after stroke via endothelial-mesenchymal transformation (EndoMT).
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by experimental data showing the role of myeloid cells and EndoMT.

claim: Decreasing the number of E-pericytes by specific knockout of the Tgfbr2 gene in ECs aggravated BBB leakage.
source: Decreasing the number of E-pericytes by specific knockout of the Tgfbr2 gene in ECs also aggravated BBB leakage and exacerbated neurological deficits.
evidence: This is an experimental finding using genetic manipulation to reduce E-pericytes.

claim: Decreasing the number of E-pericytes by specific knockout of the Tgfbr2 gene in ECs exacerbated neurological deficits.
source: Decreasing the number of E-pericytes by specific knockout of the Tgfbr2 gene in ECs also aggravated BBB leakage and exacerbated neurological deficits.
evidence: This is an experimental finding using genetic manipulation to reduce E-pericytes.

claim: EC-specific overexpression of the Tgfbr2 gene promoting E-pericytes transdifferentiation reduced BBB leakage.
source: EC-specific overexpression of the Tgfbr2 gene promoting E-pericytes transdifferentiation reduced BBB leakage and exerted neuroprotective effects.
evidence: This is an experimental finding using genetic overexpression to increase E-pericytes.

claim: EC-specific overexpression of the Tgfbr2 gene promoting E-pericytes transdifferentiation exerted neuroprotective effects.
source: EC-specific overexpression of the Tgfbr2 gene promoting E-pericytes transdifferentiation reduced BBB leakage and exerted neuroprotective effects.
evidence: This is an experimental finding using genetic overexpression to increase E-pericytes.

claim: The liver is the unique solid organ capable of precisely regulating its mass through regeneration to maintain the liver-to-body mass ratio within the optimal range required for metabolic homeostasis.
source: The liver is the unique solid organ capable of precisely regulating its mass through regeneration to maintain the liver-to-body mass ratio within the optimal range required for metabolic homeostasis (Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021; Michalopoulos and DeFrances, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on liver regeneration.

claim: Vascular repair is crucial in liver regeneration and skin wound healing because blood vessels can provide nutrients and oxygen to facilitate tissue restoration and functional recovery in the chronic stage.
source: Vascular repair is crucial in liver regeneration and skin wound healing because blood vessels can provide nutrients and oxygen to facilitate tissue restoration and functional recovery in the chronic stage (Singhal et al., 2018; Peña and Martin, 2024; Park et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on vascular repair in tissue regeneration.

claim: Stroke results in large-scale cell death because of ongoing ischemia and hypoxia.
source: Stroke results in large-scale cell death because of ongoing ischemia and hypoxia, which remains a major cause of adult disability and death (Broughton et al., 2009; Gorelick, 2019; Feigin et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on stroke pathophysiology.

claim: Stroke remains a major cause of adult disability and death.
source: Stroke results in large-scale cell death because of ongoing ischemia and hypoxia, which remains a major cause of adult disability and death (Broughton et al., 2009; Gorelick, 2019; Feigin et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on stroke epidemiology.

claim: The definitive spontaneous repairing processes in the brain remain largely unknown after stroke.
source: The definitive spontaneous repairing processes in the brain remain largely unknown after stroke, and the decoding and harnessing of these processes may accelerate brain recovery, which usually takes years.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Brain recovery after stroke usually takes years.
source: The definitive spontaneous repairing processes in the brain remain largely unknown after stroke, and the decoding and harnessing of these processes may accelerate brain recovery, which usually takes years.
evidence: This is a statement based on clinical knowledge of stroke recovery timelines.

claim: Efforts to promote brain recovery have mainly involved protective trophic factors and cell transplants designed to rescue or replace a specific population of neurons.
source: Until recently, such efforts mainly involved protective trophic factors and cell transplants designed to rescue or replace a specific population of neurons, and the results have largely been disappointing in clinical outcomes (Barker et al., 2018; Gill et al., 2003; Bartus and Johnson, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on stroke treatment approaches.

claim: The results of protective trophic factors and cell transplants for stroke have largely been disappointing in clinical outcomes.
source: Until recently, such efforts mainly involved protective trophic factors and cell transplants designed to rescue or replace a specific population of neurons, and the results have largely been disappointing in clinical outcomes (Barker et al., 2018; Gill et al., 2003; Bartus and Johnson, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on stroke treatment outcomes.

claim: Treatments to reduce neuronal death and limit acute damage are desirable by timely restoring blood vessel reperfusion in the acute phase.
source: Treatments to reduce neuronal death and limit acute damage are desirable by timely restoring blood vessel reperfusion in the acute phase (Juttler et al., 2006; Li et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on acute stroke treatment.

claim: No proven medical therapies exist for restoring cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the chronic phase.
source: No proven medical therapies exist for restoring cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the chronic phase.
evidence: This statement identifies a therapeutic gap in stroke treatment.

claim: The knowledge of brain self-repair by remedying vascular vessels after stroke in the chronic repair phase is still rare.
source: Unfortunately, the knowledge of brain self-repair by remedying vascular vessels after stroke in the chronic repair phase is still rare.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Nutrient and gas exchange occur primarily in the capillary beds, up to 90% of blood vessel length.
source: Nutrient and gas exchange occur primarily in the capillary beds, up to 90% of blood vessel length (Murrant and Fletcher, 2022; Iadecola et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on vascular physiology.

claim: Capillaries are mainly composed of endothelial cells (ECs) and pericytes, which safeguard the functions of capillary beds.
source: Capillaries are mainly composed of endothelial cells (ECs) and pericytes, which safeguard the functions of capillary beds (Trimm and Red-Horse, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on capillary structure.

claim: Pericytes rapidly exhibited apoptosis and death after stroke.
source: Pericytes rapidly exhibited apoptosis and death after stroke; nevertheless, ECs tolerated ischemia and hypoxia (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on pericyte response to stroke.

claim: ECs tolerated ischemia and hypoxia after stroke.
source: Pericytes rapidly exhibited apoptosis and death after stroke; nevertheless, ECs tolerated ischemia and hypoxia (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on EC response to stroke.

claim: When pericytes are lost, the functions of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and CBF are destroyed.
source: When pericytes are lost, the functions of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and CBF are destroyed.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of pericyte function.

claim: The BBB serves as a selectively permeable interface that precisely regulates substance exchange between the circulation and the central nervous system (CNS), thereby maintaining the specialized microenvironment essential for proper neuronal signaling.
source: The BBB serves as a selectively permeable interface that precisely regulates substance exchange between the circulation and the central nervous system (CNS), thereby maintaining the specialized microenvironment essential for proper neuronal signaling (Ding et al., 2023; Armulik et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on BBB function.

claim: Effective CBF is essential for cell survival in the brain after stroke.
source: Effective CBF is essential for cell survival in the brain after stroke.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of cerebral perfusion and cell survival.

claim: The prevention of BBB leakage and the decrease of CBF due to pericyte loss is important for vascular and neurological functions after stroke.
source: The prevention of BBB leakage and the decrease of CBF due to pericyte loss is important for vascular and neurological functions after stroke.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the established roles of pericytes in BBB and CBF maintenance.

claim: Certain ECs in the embryo undergo hematopoietic transition, giving rise to multi-lineage hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, which are crucial for developing the blood system.
source: Certain ECs in the embryo undergo hematopoietic transition, giving rise to multi-lineage hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, which are crucial for developing the blood system (Yokomizo and Suda, 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition.

claim: ECs can undergo EndoMT, acquiring mesenchymal properties.
source: ECs can undergo EndoMT, acquiring mesenchymal properties.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of endothelial plasticity.

claim: EndoMT is important in various pathological conditions, such as fibrosis and cancer.
source: The process is important in various pathological conditions, such as fibrosis and cancer (Xu and Kovacic, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on EndoMT in disease.

claim: Endocardial ECs are progenitors of pericytes and smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the murine embryonic heart via EndoMT.
source: Endocardial ECs are progenitors of pericytes and smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the murine embryonic heart via EndoMT (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on cardiac development.

claim: Protein C receptor-expressing (Procr+) ECs would give rise to de novo formation of ECs and pericytes in the mammary gland.
source: Protein C receptor-expressing (Procr+) ECs would give rise to de novo formation of ECs and pericytes in the mammary gland (Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on mammary gland development.

claim: In the acute and subacute phases after stroke, myeloid cells were dominant immune cells entering the brain parenchyma.
source: In the acute and subacute phases after stroke, myeloid cells were dominant immune cells entering the brain parenchyma (Jiang and McCullough, 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on post-stroke immune response.

claim: Most myeloid cells could not occupy the ischemic brain for a long time and faded away by releasing various factors, including pro-inflammatory, anti-inflammatory, and trophic factors.
source: Most myeloid cells could not occupy the ischemic brain for a long time and faded away by releasing various factors, including pro-inflammatory, anti-inflammatory, and trophic factors (Beuker et al., 2022; Shichita et al., 2023; Gliem et al., 2012; Sas et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on myeloid cell dynamics after stroke.

claim: Blocking myeloid cell recruitment using anti-CCR2 antibody and CCR2 gene knockout mice impaired long-term spontaneous behavioral recovery after stroke via reducing anti-inflammatory macrophages and angiogenesis.
source: Blocking myeloid cell recruitment using anti-CCR2 antibody and CCR2 gene knockout mice impaired long-term spontaneous behavioral recovery after stroke via reducing anti-inflammatory macrophages and angiogenesis (Fang et al., 2018; Pedragosa et al., 2020; Wattananit et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on myeloid cells and stroke recovery.

claim: In mice subjected to distal middle cerebral artery occlusion (dMCAO), TGFβ1 was predominantly co-localized with CD68+ activated microglia and macrophages.
source: In mice subjected to distal middle cerebral artery occlusion (dMCAO) (Doyle et al., 2010), TGFβ1 was predominantly co-localized with CD68+ activated microglia and macrophages.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on TGFβ1 expression after stroke.

claim: TGFβ1 contributed to angiogenic pathogenesis in human stroke patients.
source: Importantly, TGFβ1 contributed to angiogenic pathogenesis in human stroke patients (Krupinski et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on TGFβ1 in human stroke.

claim: TGFβ is the main driver of EndoMT, which is involved in endothelial-to-pericytic transition in the murine embryonic heart and mammary gland.
source: At the same time, TGFβ is the main driver of EndoMT, which is involved in endothelial-to-pericytic transition in the murine embryonic heart and mammary gland (Cooley et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature on TGFβ and EndoMT.

claim: Transdifferentiation of ECs into E-pericytes replenishes the pericyte pool, critically contributing to BBB restoration and brain self-repair after stroke.
source: Transdifferentiation of ECs into E-pericytes replenishes the pericyte pool, critically contributing to BBB restoration and brain self-repair after stroke.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: In the MCAO model, ischemic injury triggered endothelial-to-pericytic transition, driven by myeloid cells via the TGFβ1-TGFβR2-EndoMT pathway.
source: In the MCAO model, ischemic injury triggered endothelial-to-pericytic transition, driven by myeloid cells via the TGFβ1-TGFβR2-EndoMT pathway.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The dynamic changes in E-pericyte numbers directly influenced BBB integrity and long-term functional recovery.
source: The dynamic changes in E-pericyte numbers directly influenced BBB integrity and long-term functional recovery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental manipulations of E-pericyte numbers in the study.

claim: CD13+ pericytes and CD31+ ECs exhibited TUNEL positivity in brain parenchyma in the stroke model.
source: In the stroke model, CD13+ pericytes and CD31+ ECs exhibited TUNEL positivity in brain parenchyma.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Only half of the pericytes survived at reperfusion 2 days (RP2D), while over 80% of ECs survived.
source: Moreover, only half of the pericytes survived at reperfusion 2 days (RP2D), while over 80% of ECs survived (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The number of CD13+ pericytes on capillary decreased at RP2D but then increased at RP7D after stroke.
source: The number of CD13+ pericytes on capillary also decreased at RP2D but then increased at RP7D after stroke (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study shown in Figures 1B and C.

claim: Flow cytometry revealed that the number of pericytes significantly decreased, from 100% on the contralateral side to approximately 50% on the ipsilateral side at RP2D, but gradually increased following reperfusion after stroke.
source: Flow cytometry also revealed that the number of pericytes significantly decreased, from 100% on the contralateral side to approximately 50% on the ipsilateral side at RP2D, but gradually increased following reperfusion after stroke (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from flow cytometry shown in Figures 1D and E.

claim: There was a 68.1% increase in the pericyte pool from RP2D to RP34D.
source: Overall, there was a 68.1% increase in the pericyte pool from RP2D to RP34D and a 40.5% increase in total pericytes at RP34D (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There was a 40.5% increase in total pericytes at RP34D.
source: Overall, there was a 68.1% increase in the pericyte pool from RP2D to RP34D and a 40.5% increase in total pericytes at RP34D (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cell proliferation occurred mainly within the first 3 days after stroke.
source: EdU was injected into the mice at different times to identify proliferating pericytes and ECs (Figure 1F), and it was found that cell proliferation occurred mainly within the first 3 days after stroke (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from EdU labeling shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Both pericytes and ECs underwent self-proliferation.
source: Both pericytes and ECs underwent self-proliferation (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from EdU labeling shown in Figure 1H.

claim: EdU+ ECs accounted for fewer than 10% of all ECs.
source: EdU+ ECs accounted for fewer than 10% of all ECs, and EdU+ pericytes accounted for approximately 12.9% of all pericytes (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from EdU labeling shown in Figure 1I.

claim: EdU+ pericytes accounted for approximately 12.9% of all pericytes.
source: EdU+ ECs accounted for fewer than 10% of all ECs, and EdU+ pericytes accounted for approximately 12.9% of all pericytes (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from EdU labeling shown in Figure 1I.

claim: EdU+ pericytes and ECs ceased proliferating after RP7D.
source: EdU+ pericytes and ECs ceased proliferating after RP7D (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from EdU labeling shown in Figure 1J.

claim: 12.9% of the pericytes originated from self-proliferation at RP34D.
source: Thus, 12.9% of the pericytes originated from self-proliferation at RP34D, whereas the origin of the other 27.6% of new pericytes remained unknown.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the EdU labeling data.

claim: The origin of 27.6% of new pericytes at RP34D remained unknown.
source: Thus, 12.9% of the pericytes originated from self-proliferation at RP34D, whereas the origin of the other 27.6% of new pericytes remained unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap that the study aims to address.

claim: EGFP signals were restricted to cells expressing EC markers (CD31+, ERG+, GLUT1+, and VE-Cadherin+) within the brain parenchyma in iECs;Ai47 mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining showed that EGFP signals were restricted to cells expressing EC markers (CD31+, ERG+, GLUT1+, and VE-Cadherin+) within the brain parenchyma (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1l).
evidence: This is an experimental validation of the lineage tracing system shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The EGFP signal did not represent pericyte (CD13+, PDGFRβ+, α-SMA+, and NG2+ cells) cells in the brain parenchyma of iECs;Ai47 mice.
source: The EGFP signal did not represent pericyte (CD13+, PDGFRβ+, α-SMA+, and NG2+ cells) cells in the brain parenchyma (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This is an experimental validation of the lineage tracing system shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Vascular ECs in the brain parenchyma were specifically labeled by EGFP from the homeostasis of iECs;Ai47 mice.
source: Therefore, vascular ECs in the brain parenchyma were specifically labeled by EGFP from the homeostasis of iECs;Ai47 mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation experiments.

claim: 3568 cells were obtained from the sham group, 4147 cells from the MCAO group at RP7D, and 5070 cells from the MCAO group at RP34D after scRNA-seq.
source: After sorting by 10X Genomics and quality control (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), 3568 cells were obtained from the sham group, 4147 cells from the MCAO group at RP7D, and 5070 cells from the MCAO group at RP34D.
evidence: This is a description of the scRNA-seq dataset.

claim: 10 major cell types were identified in scRNA-seq: arterial ECs, venous ECs (2 types), capillary ECs, capillary-venous ECs, SMCs, pericytes, fibroblasts, microglia, and ependymal cells.
source: Different markers were used to identify the cell types based on literature (Vanlandewijck et al., 2018; Kalucka et al., 2020; Garcia-Bonilla et al., 2024; Figure 2B) and found 10 major cell types: arterial ECs, venous ECs (2 types), capillary ECs, capillary-venous ECs, SMCs, pericytes, fibroblasts, microglia, and ependymal cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: ECs accounted for over 90% of all cells in the scRNA-seq dataset for different groups.
source: ECs accounted for over 90% of all cells for different groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from scRNA-seq shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The proportions of three cell types (pericytes, fibroblasts, and microglia) markedly increased after MCAO.
source: The number of cells was calculated in the sham group and MCAO group at RP7D and RP34D, and the proportions of three cell types (pericytes, fibroblasts, and microglia) markedly increased (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from scRNA-seq shown in Figure 2E and supplementary figure.

claim: Pseudotime trajectory analysis suggested that the developmental trajectory was from ECs to pericytes and arterial ECs.
source: Pseudotime trajectory analysis suggested that the developmental trajectory was from ECs to pericytes and arterial ECs (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from computational analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: scRNA-seq results indicated that ECs might turn into pericyte-like cells after stroke.
source: Thus, the scRNA-seq results indicated that ECs might turn into pericyte-like cells after stroke.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: CBF was reduced by ~80% after MCAO, confirming successful induction of ischemia in mice.
source: Laser speckle analysis showed that CBF was reduced by ~80% after MCAO, confirming successful induction of ischemia in mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental validation of the stroke model shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Some EGFP+ cells detached from blood vessels, had long processes with secondary branches, and showed no expression of EC markers (CD31, ERG, GLUT1, and VE-Cadherin) at RP34D after stroke.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed the presence of EGFP+ cells in the ischemic area at RP34D. Some cells detached from blood vessels, had long processes with secondary branches, and showed no expression of EC markers (CD31, ERG, GLUT1, and VE-Cadherin) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figure.

claim: EGFP+ CD31- cells expressed classic pericyte markers (CD13, PDGFRβ, and NG2).
source: Moreover, the EGFP+ CD31- cells expressed classic pericyte markers (CD13, PDGFRβ, and NG2) (Figure 3A–C), which also indicated ECs might turn into pericyte-like cells after stroke.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from immunofluorescence shown in Figures 3A-C.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs expressed fibroblast marker PDGFRɑ at RP34D.
source: In the stroke model, EGFP+ non-ECs expressed fibroblast marker PDGFRɑ at RP34D (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3D.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs did not express vimentin.
source: However, EGFP+ non-ECs did not express vimentin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which indicates that the EGFP+ non-ECs were not fibroblasts, but pericyte-like cells that expressed certain proteins involved in matrix remodeling.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from immunofluorescence shown in supplementary figure.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs were not fibroblasts, but pericyte-like cells that expressed certain proteins involved in matrix remodeling.
source: However, EGFP+ non-ECs did not express vimentin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which indicates that the EGFP+ non-ECs were not fibroblasts, but pericyte-like cells that expressed certain proteins involved in matrix remodeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunofluorescence data.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs did not express microglia markers (Iba1 and CD68).
source: Moreover, EGFP+ non-ECs did not express microglia markers (Iba1 and CD68) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), which indicated that EGFP+ non-ECs were not microglia.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from immunofluorescence shown in supplementary figure.

claim: 27.8% of total vascular pericytes were EGFP+ non-ECs located on vessels.
source: The proportions of EGFP+ non-ECs located on vessels were as follows: 27.8% of total vascular pericytes (Figure 3E), 27.5% of total EGFP+ non-ECs (Figure 3F), 38.1% of migrating EGFP+ non-ECs (Figure 3G), 22.45% of total pericytes (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 27.5% of total EGFP+ non-ECs were located on vessels.
source: The proportions of EGFP+ non-ECs located on vessels were as follows: 27.8% of total vascular pericytes (Figure 3E), 27.5% of total EGFP+ non-ECs (Figure 3F), 38.1% of migrating EGFP+ non-ECs (Figure 3G), 22.45% of total pericytes (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3F.

claim: 38.1% of migrating EGFP+ non-ECs were located on vessels.
source: The proportions of EGFP+ non-ECs located on vessels were as follows: 27.8% of total vascular pericytes (Figure 3E), 27.5% of total EGFP+ non-ECs (Figure 3F), 38.1% of migrating EGFP+ non-ECs (Figure 3G), 22.45% of total pericytes (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3G.

claim: 22.45% of total pericytes were EGFP+ non-ECs.
source: The proportions of EGFP+ non-ECs located on vessels were as follows: 27.8% of total vascular pericytes (Figure 3E), 27.5% of total EGFP+ non-ECs (Figure 3F), 38.1% of migrating EGFP+ non-ECs (Figure 3G), 22.45% of total pericytes (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3H.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs began to appear at RP7D, and their proportion peaked at RP14D.
source: EGFP+ non-ECs began to appear at RP7D, and their proportion peaked at RP14D (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from flow cytometry shown in Figure 3I.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs survived over 514 days after MCAO.
source: Furthermore, the EGFP+ non-ECs survived over 514 days after MCAO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figure.

claim: At RP8D, EGFP+ non-ECs expressed PDGFRα and vimentin but not CD13 and NG2.
source: At RP8D, EGFP+ non-ECs expressed PDGFRα (Figure 3J) and vimentin (Figure 3K) but not CD13 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) and NG2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from immunofluorescence shown in figures.

claim: GO and KEGG analyses revealed that EGFP+ non-ECs expressed genes involved in matrix synthesis, matrix remodeling, and ossification at RP8D.
source: GO and KEGG analyses also revealed that EGFP+ non-ECs expressed genes involved in matrix synthesis, matrix remodeling, and ossification at RP8D (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatics analysis shown in Figures 3L and M.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs presented the characteristics of fibroblast-like cells at RP8D and pericyte-like cells at RP34D.
source: EGFP+ non-ECs presented the characteristics of fibroblast-like cells at RP8D and pericyte-like cells at RP34D.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal expression patterns observed.

claim: The majority of the EGFP+ non-ECs were located in the penumbra.
source: The majority of the EGFP+ non-ECs were located in the penumbra (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), and they were not proliferating, as they were not labeled by EdU at RP34D (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J), which indicated that EGFP+ non-ECs were converted from ECs via transdifferentiation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figure.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs were not proliferating, as they were not labeled by EdU at RP34D.
source: The majority of the EGFP+ non-ECs were located in the penumbra (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), and they were not proliferating, as they were not labeled by EdU at RP34D (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J), which indicated that EGFP+ non-ECs were converted from ECs via transdifferentiation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figure.

claim: EGFP+ non-ECs were converted from ECs via transdifferentiation.
source: The majority of the EGFP+ non-ECs were located in the penumbra (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), and they were not proliferating, as they were not labeled by EdU at RP34D (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J), which indicated that EGFP+ non-ECs were converted from ECs via transdifferentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of EdU labeling and lineage tracing data.

claim: Fewer than 1% of nucleated cells in bone marrow (BM) were labeled with EGFP in iECs;Ai47 mice, mainly myeloid cells.
source: In iECs;Ai47 mice, fewer than 1% of nucleated cells in bone marrow (BM) were labeled with EGFP, main myeloid cells (Gentek et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation about the lineage tracing system with citation support.

claim: Macrophages could invade the brain and develop pericytes in the early phase of vascular development in the CNS.
